title: The month of Sawan
hookLine: in Sawan the bride blossoms who loves His lotus feet (Barah Maha, ang 134)

lines: THE SMELL OF THE FIRST RAIN.
cards: Anyone who has lived through a North Indian summer remembers the first real rain. The smell comes before the drops: wet dust, sharp and sweet. Then the sky opens.

Kids run into the street. Peacocks call from the fields. Within days, cracked brown ground turns green, swings go up in the trees of Punjabi villages, and girls and women gather to sing the songs of Teeyan.
Sawan, July into August, is when the whole land seems to exhale. And in the folk barah maha, it's the month the waiting bride feels most alive, and most alone.

teach.b: The Sawan stanza is on ang 134. In paraphrase: in Sawan, the bride blossoms who loves the lotus feet of the Lord. Sarsee: she blossoms, she flourishes, the way the land does when the rain comes.
Her mind and body are dyed in true love; the Name alone is her support.
Then a contrast: the pleasures of poison, as the stanza calls them, are false, and everything seen of them turns to ash. Then the rain image, turned inside out.

teach.h: A DROP OF THE LORD'S NECTAR.
teach.b: The drop of the Lord's nectar is beautiful, and those who meet the holy ones drink it in. The forests and meadows are refreshed by the One, the all-powerful, the infinite. Look at what Guru Arjan does with the monsoon.
In the folk songs, the rain makes the separated woman ache: everyone else is together under the swings. Here, the rain is what happens to the soul that loves the One.

teach.h: THE SOUL IS THE LAND; LOVE IS THE RAIN.
teach.b: She's the land; the love is the rain. And she doesn't just survive the season; she blossoms.
Sawan is the first month in this Barah Maha that sounds almost like arrival. It isn't all joy; the warning about false pleasures turning to ash is still there. But the main image is green.
After Jeth and Asarh, where the lesson was bowing and keeping the One near, Sawan shows what that nearness looks like when it rains.
The lotus feet, charan kamal, is an old and tender image in Indian devotion, and Gurbani uses it often: the Beloved's feet, soft as a lotus, are where the devotee comes to rest.

how: On the sangrand of Sawan, many gurdwaras read the Sawan stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, while in Punjab the monsoon month is also marked by the folk festival of Teeyan.

games.q: the monsoon has come, swings are up in the trees, and the folk songs say the waiting bride aches. what does Guru Arjan's Sawan stanza say?
o: the bride who loves the Lord's lotus feet blossoms.
she should stay indoors until the rain stops.
games.why: in Sawan, the bride blossoms who loves the lotus feet. the soul is the land; the love is the rain.

practice: Watch rain at a window if it's falling, or pour a glass of water slowly and watch it fill, or simply picture the first drops darkening dry dust.
Breathe slowly, and let the picture soften something in you that's been dry, watered without needing to understand it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each slow breath.

wordCard.voice: Sawan. The monsoon month: the bride who loves the Lord's lotus feet blossoms, like land under the rain, and drinks the drop of nectar.
